figures.caption: Fig. 1: CTA tile allocation under static vs. routing-aware dispatch for E=16, S=16. Horizontal lines within each bar mark tile boundaries; each tile maps to one CTA. Top row (static): dispatch always uses bm=16 (optimal at β=1.0), incurring excessive padding waste (red) as routing becomes skewed (β=0.2: 60% waste). Bottom row (RaMP): adapts bm to the routing distribution, reducing waste to 20% (orange) at β=0.2 by selecting bm=4 (more, smaller tiles). At uniform routing (β=1.0), both choose the same configuration.

Fig. 8: (a) Cost model predicted time for four bm values on OLMoE vs. batch size S. At small S, bm=8 achieves the lowest cost (minimal padding); at large S, bm=64 wins (fewer waves). (b) Wave staircase for bm=16: time jumps discretely at wave boundaries (SM=132).
TABLE IV: Cost model regret (%) vs. exhaustive search (50- iteration median, 24 test points per model). Unseen models were profiled from scratch with zero prior knowledge.
TABLE V: Routing-aware (RA) vs. static dispatch. Static selects the best config at β=1.0. RA uses the cost model with the actual routing histogram. Same kernel binary; only dispatch differs.

Fig. 6: Split-K fills idle SMs at sub-wave operating points. (a) Standard kernel: 3 CTAs occupy 3 of 8 SMs (ω=0.38, 62% idle). (b) Split-K=4: K-reduction partitioned across 4 CTAs per expert, yielding 12 CTAs that fill both waves (ω=1.5, all SMs active).

Fig. 7: Regime classification of 8 MoE models in the (λ, ρ) plane. Models below ρc=200 are overhead-dominated (Regime A); models above are compute-scaling (Regime B) where GROUP M swizzle is essential. Blue circles: 5 known models; orange squares: 3 unseen test models.
